WEEK 1 LAB · FILES, RULES, AND RELATIONSHIPS
:::

# What is this table really claiming?

A tidy table can hide repeated information, unstated assumptions, and rules that exist only in people's heads. In this lab, your job is to make those hidden pieces visible before proposing a better model.

::: {.lesson-question}
**Lab question:** Which information, assumptions, and rules are only implied by the file, and which should become explicit parts of a data system?
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Reasonable inference is part of the work

You are allowed to speculate about what the table seems to mean. In fact, that is part of the point. Just distinguish clearly among:

- what the file explicitly states;
- what a careful human reader would reasonably infer; and
- what would still need clarification before a database design could enforce it.
:::

::: {.activity-meta-grid}
::: {.activity-meta-card}
### Time

Approximately 35-45 minutes
:::

::: {.activity-meta-card}
### Collaboration

Groups of two or three
:::

::: {.activity-meta-card}
### Submission

One short artifact per group
:::
:::

Before beginning, read the Week 1 lecture, [Is a database just a glorified spreadsheet?](../lectures/week-01-database-or-spreadsheet.qmd), through the discussion of spreadsheets and databases.

## Learning goals

By completing this lab, you should be able to:

1. identify when the same real-world information is repeated across multiple rows;
2. distinguish information about sessions, students, courses, and tutors;
3. surface assumptions that a human reader can infer but the file does not actually enforce;
4. expose update, insertion, and deletion problems in a flat representation; and
5. sketch a first model that separates entities, identifiers, and relationships.

## Scenario and data

A tutoring center keeps all session records in one spreadsheet.

| session_id | student_netid | student_name | course_code | course_title | tutor_netid | tutor_name | session_start | room_code |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | acb12 | Ava Brooks | CSCI127 | Joy and Beauty of Data | tlopez | T. Lopez | 2026-09-03 15:00 | SS 120 |
| 2 | acb12 | Ava Brooks | CSCI127 | Joy and Beauty of Data | tlopez | T. Lopez | 2026-09-10 15:00 | SS 120 |
| 3 | jkm44 | Jordan Kim | MATH152 | Calculus II | rpatel | Rina Patel | 2026-09-03 16:00 | LA 011 |
| 4 | acb12 | Ava Brookes | CSCI127 | Joy & Beauty of Data | tlopez | T. Lopez | 2026-09-17 15:00 | SS 120 |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Do not clean the data yet

Your goal is to discover what the current representation permits. If you "fix" row 4 immediately, you will hide the design problem that produced it.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What counts as repeated information?

Repeated information is not just a value that appears more than once. It is the same information about the same real-world thing appearing in multiple rows.

Examples:

- "`acb12` is the identifier for Ava Brooks" is information about a student.
- "`CSCI127` has the title Joy and Beauty of Data" is information about a course.
- "`tlopez` refers to tutor T. Lopez" is information about a tutor.

That information repeats because the file stores it again every time a session is recorded.
:::

## Part A — Separate row information from repeated information

Using the four-row table:

1. List at least four examples of repeated information as complete sentences.
2. Identify at least two contradictions or near-contradictions in the file.
3. For each column below, decide what kind of thing it describes most directly.
4. Name two assumptions or inferences a human reader is likely making that the file itself does not prove.

| Item to analyze | Your answer | Evidence in the file | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repeated information | | | |
| Repeated information | | | |
| A contradiction or near-contradiction | | | |
| A human assumption | | | |
| A human assumption | | | |

Now classify these fields:

| Field | Session | Student | Course | Tutor | Not enough information |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `session_start` | □ | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `student_name` | □ | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `course_title` | □ | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `tutor_netid` | □ | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `room_code` | □ | □ | □ | □ | □ |

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** If you wrote "Ava Brooks appears three times," revise it into a clearer statement about repeated information. What exactly is the file saying each time that name appears?
:::

## Part B — Stress the representation

For each failure below, describe the smallest edit or sequence of edits that would produce it.

| Failure to produce | Minimal change | Why the file cannot prevent it |
|---|---|---|
| The same student appears under two names | | |
| The same course code appears with two titles | | |
| A session refers to a tutor who is not otherwise known | | |
| Deleting one row removes the only known fact about a tutor or course | | |
| Two sessions assign the same tutor at the same time | | |
| A row uses a value whose datatype or format should be invalid | | |

::: {.callout-question appearance="simple"}
## Think about rules, not just typos

Which failures are about inconsistency? Which are about missing relationships? Which are about the absence of datatype or formatting rules?
:::

## Part C — Propose a first model

Sketch boxes for the distinct kinds of things you believe exist. Add a possible identifier to each box and draw the relationships among them. You may draw on paper and attach a clear image, use a diagramming tool, or use Mermaid. Formal ER notation is not required yet.

Your sketch should probably address at least some of these questions:

- Is a tutoring session the same thing as a student? A course? A tutor?
- Can one student appear in many sessions?
- Can one tutor work with many students?
- Is `course_title` a fact about a session or a fact about a course?
- Does `room_code` identify a room entity or merely record a label?

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** Every box should complete the sentence "This is one _____." Every line should complete the sentence "One _____ can be related to _____."
:::

Below your sketch, list at least two assumptions that would need clarification before the design could be considered correct.

## Part D — Defend one rule

Choose one rule that belongs in the data system rather than only in written instructions. State:

1. the rule in plain language;
2. a minimal example that violates it;
3. why the violation matters; and
4. a database mechanism that might enforce it, even if you do not yet know the SQL syntax.

Possible rules include:

- one `student_netid` identifies one student;
- one `course_code` identifies one course title;
- one tutor cannot be assigned to two sessions at the same time;
- `session_start` must be a valid date-time value; or
- a session must refer to an existing student, course, and tutor.

## What to submit

Submit one group artifact containing:

- the names of all participating group members;
- the completed observations from Part A;
- the failure cases from Part B;
- the model sketch and assumptions from Part C; and
- the rule defense from Part D.

The artifact may be a short document, a rendered Quarto page, or a clearly legible scan, as directed by the instructor. A concise submission is expected; completeness and reasoning matter more than visual polish.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Before submitting

Confirm that another group could identify your repeated information as sentences, understand your proposed entities and relationships, and construct the invalid example your chosen rule would reject.
:::

## Completion criteria

A complete submission:

- identifies repeated information as claims about real-world things, not merely as duplicated strings;
- distinguishes at least three kinds of information in the file;
- separates direct evidence from reasonable inference;
- surfaces both inconsistency problems and missing-rule problems;
- proposes identifiers and relationships rather than merely regrouping columns; and
- states assumptions instead of presenting the sketch as the only possible answer.
